question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on her attendance at the recent British-Irish Association annual conference.
reply:
I attended the annual British Irish Association conference in Oxford on 4 September which was held under Chatham House rules.
I was pleased to deliver opening remarks and to participate in an interactive question and answer session with participants. In my remarks, I spoke about how relations across these islands are being reshaped by the changes we are seeing in the international environment and the shared challenges these changes present us all.
I recalled the ambitious agenda for bilateral relations between the Irish and UK government, in the shape of the UK-Ireland Joint Statement.
I also spoke about our work to unlock the full potential of the Good Friday Agreement through the work of the North South bodies and through the Shared Island Initiative. I discussed the implementation of the Joint Framework on Legacy, which we agreed with the UK Government last year.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she and her Department have taken diplomatically at EU and UN level to pursue global action on climate commitments and the Paris Agreement following the heatwaves, flooding, and other extreme weather events globally in recent months.
reply:

As EU Presidency, Ireland is leading engagement with EU Member States, the European Commission and international partners in advance of COP31 in Antalya in November. We are working to build consensus around outcomes on emissions reduction, adaptation, climate finance and loss and damage, with the objective of keeping the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal within reach.
At the United Nations, including during UN General Assembly High-Level Week, we have engaged with UN partners, fellow Member States and vulnerable countries on preparations for COP31. Ireland consistently advocates for the prioritisation of adaptation finance for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States, with a particular emphasis on grant-based support.
This is reflected across Ireland's own international climate finance with, 89% of which supports adaptation, helping vulnerable communities to strengthen their resilience and prepare for a changing climate.

reply:

Ireland’s total Official Development Assistance (ODA) amounted to €1.88 billion in 2025, representing 0.44% of Gross National Income (GNI). question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which she has raised the issue to advance the case for Irish reunification internationally.
reply:
The position of the Government on Irish re-unification is determined by Article 3 of the Constitution, as amended by the people in 1998 to incorporate the framework set out in the Good Friday Agreement.
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the functioning of all of its institutions.
In my discussions with international partners, I am heartened that there is a continued interest in the peace process and on furthering reconciliation in Northern Ireland today.
Securing the peace through the Good Friday Agreement would not have been possible without the support of those international partners.
Our commitment to unlocking the full potential of the Agreement, includes addressing the legacy of the Troubles and through the Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035. Our whole-of-government approach is building a more connected, prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South. In the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations within the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has assessed whether Ireland is out of step with other European Union member states in not maintaining a trade or representative office in Taiwan; and if consideration has been given to reopening an Irish Trade and Cultural Office in Taipei to strengthen economic, trade, cultural and links with Taiwan.
reply:
Ireland, along with our EU partners, adheres to the One China Policy. This means that we recognise the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China, and that we do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan. However, the absence of diplomatic of relations does not preclude the development of economic, cultural and people-to-people connections.
My Department has never maintained an office in Taipei. IDA Ireland, the agency responsible for attracting foreign direct investment to Ireland, previously had an office in Taipei but it was closed in 2011 solely based on business reasons. IDA Ireland now manages the Taiwanese market from its Singapore office, and Enterprise Ireland, the agency responsible for enterprise development, manages the market from its office in Hong Kong.
I am aware that some EU Member States have trade offices in Taipei, and I note that the EU has maintained its European Economic and Trade Office in Taipei since 2003. However, it is important to note that decisions on the opening of new offices by the Government are taken on the basis of need and how best to promote our own interests abroad rather than to match the approach of other countries.
There are currently no plans to establish a trade and cultural office in Taipei. The establishment of new offices is always kept under review. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if Ireland is advancing proposals for the reform of United Nations structures.
reply:
Ireland supports the ongoing UN80 reform initiative launched by UN Secretary-General Guterres in 2025. The initiative aims to strengthen the effectiveness, accountability and representativeness of the UN system amid shrinking resources and rising needs.
Ireland believes that any reforms must serve to strengthen and protect the United Nations' capacity to deliver across the three pillars of Peace and Security, Sustainable Development, and Human Rights, while remaining firmly grounded in the principles of the UN Charter.
Together with our EU partners, Ireland continues to engage actively across all three work-streams of UN80. This includes initiatives to strengthen coordination, coherence and delivery across the UN, via reforms of programmes and structures.
Ireland also continues to advocate for institutional reforms, including reform of the UN Security Council. Ireland has consistently called for the veto power held by the Permanent Five members of the Security Council to be abolished. Ireland has also been clear that Council reform must address the unjust under-representation of Africa and other under-represented regions on the Council and safeguard the right of small states, including Small Island Developing States, to serve on the Council.
My Department will continue to engage on the UN80 process to ensure that Ireland's values and interests are protected and advanced.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if the Government will be maintaining or increasing current levels of foreign aid funding in budget 2027.
reply:

The Government remains committed to the UN target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). GAC Ministers will hold a discussion on the state of play on the rule of law in Hungary and are expected to approve Council conclusions on the importance of inclusive democratic participation. question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views that there are infringements on the right to protest in Germany in relation to the right of people to protest in solidarity with the Palestinian people.
reply:
The promotion and protection of human rights, including the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, are vital elements of Ireland’s foreign policy. question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has begun any internal planning concerning future constitutional change.
reply:
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the function of all of its institutions.
Our commitment is backed by our Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035.
The Initiative is enabling the largest-ever programme of all-island investment across all sectors, to build a more connected island, in terms of infrastructure, services, our economy and, crucially, between people.
The Shared Island Initiative is just one part of our work to promote peace and reconciliation on this island, work that also includes my Department's Reconciliation Fund, which awards grants to organisations working to build better relations within and between traditions in Northern Ireland, between North and South, and between Ireland and Britain. My Department also supports and provides the Dublin Secretariat for the International Fund for Ireland which continues to do important work in Northern Ireland and the border counties.
The Government is working to build a more prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South, and in the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations, in accordance with the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on discussions regarding Moldova joining the European Union.
reply:
Ireland strongly supports EU enlargement, which is a key priority of our EU Presidency.
Moldova applied for EU membership in 2022 and opened accession negotiations in 2024. After completing the screening process, Moldova opened the first two negotiating clusters - Cluster 1 on Fundamentals and Clusters 6 on External Relations – in June and July respectively.
In July, during the first month of our Presidency, Ireland secured significant progress on the enlargement file, holding the highest number of accession conferences in a single day since 2002. In addition to opening cluster 6 with both Ukraine and Moldova, we facilitated the closure of two additional chapters with Montenegro as well as the closure of the first three negotiating chapters with Albania.
Last year, the European Commission's Enlargement Report highlighted that Moldova has made the most one-year progress of all the candidates over the reporting period. I am very conscious of the efforts that Moldova is making to meet the challenge of aligning their laws with the EU acquis, despite the ongoing hybrid threats and external interference they are facing.
As confirmed by the European Commission, Moldova, as well as Ukraine, is technically ready to open all negotiating clusters. As Presidency, Ireland will continue to engage with other Member States to secure the unanimity required for the opening of all remaining clusters with both Moldova and Ukraine.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of staff that are currently accredited to the embassy of the Russian Federation.
reply:
Despite Ireland's fundamental disagreement with the actions taken by the Russian Federation since its unjustified and illegal full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Government's view is that diplomatic channels between Ireland and the Russian Federation should remain open.
This is in the interests of our citizens, in Russia and in the four Central Asian countries to which Ireland is accredited via our Embassy in Moscow. This also allows us to continue to formally convey the Government's strong objection to the illegal and unwarranted war of aggression by Russia against Ukraine.
The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 identifies three categories of staff of a diplomatic mission: diplomatic staff, administrative and technical staff and service staff.
There are currently 17 staff members at the Embassy of the Russian Federation in Ireland who have been notified to my Department under Article 10 of the Convention - six Diplomats and 11 Administrative and Technical staff. The current number of staff accredited to the Embassy is taken at a point in time, and minor increases or decreases in numbers may relate to vacancies that arise over time.
Prior to Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine there were a total of 30 staff at the Embassy, 14 diplomats and 16 Administrative and Technical staff.

reply:
Building Regulations set out the legal requirements for the construction of new buildings, extensions to existing buildings, material alterations and certain material changes of use to existing buildings. They are performance based and technology neutral.
A minimum renewable energy ratio for all new dwellings is required, and already includes solar energy systems and alternative renewable energy technologies as defined in the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive. The renewable energy provided by these systems is taken account of for the purpose of Building Regulations compliance.
The primary responsibility for compliance with the requirements of the Building Regulations rests with the designers, builders and owners of buildings. Technical Guidance Document L presents several compliance examples, including solar energy systems.
The EU Energy Performance of Buildings Regulations 2019 introduced the Nearly Zero Energy Building, or NZEB standard, for all new dwellings from 31st October 2020.

- at least 65% less carbon emissions;
- at least 70% less primary energy use; and
- at least 20% of their energy use comes from renewable sources.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the role envisioned by his Department for artificial intelligence and quantum computing in predicting and responding to climate and weather events.
reply:
